summary: Proposes an additional response format for OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection, secured as a JSON Web Token. This lets the server sign the answer about a token.

eli5.summary: When an app asks whether a pass is still good, the answer can come in a sealed, signed envelope so nobody can fake it.

questions: jwt response for oauth token introspection
how to request a signed introspection response
subtitle: How an OAuth authorization server can answer token introspection with a signed, optionally encrypted JWT.

tldr.problem: The standard token introspection response is a plain JSON object, but some resource servers need stronger assurance that the authorization server really issued it, for example when the server takes liability for the content.
tldr.mechanism: The resource server asks with Accept: application/token-introspection+jwt, and the authorization server returns a JWT whose token_introspection claim holds the normal introspection members. The JWT is signed and optionally encrypted as a Nested JWT.
tldr.outcome: Resource servers get a verifiable, optionally confidential answer about a token. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9701 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Sign an Introspection Response
sections.content:
RFC 7662 lets a protected resource (the resource server, RS) ask an OAuth 2.0 authorization server (AS) about the state of an access token. This makes opaque access tokens workable in an interoperable way. The answer in RFC 7662 is a plain JSON object.

Some use cases need more. The RS may require stronger assurance that the AS issued the response, including cases where the AS assumes liability for its content. The RFC's example is an RS using verified personal data to create certificates that are used for qualified electronic signatures. RFC 9701 extends the introspection endpoint so it can return a signed JWT (RFC 7519) instead.
sections.eli5: Normally the answer is a note anyone could have scribbled. Sometimes you need a note with an official stamp that proves who wrote it.

sections.title: Managing Resource Servers
sections.content:
The AS and RS keep a strong, two-way trust relationship. Because the introspection endpoint now conveys security data and possibly privacy-sensitive data, the AS MUST be able to identify, authenticate and authorize resource servers. It MUST also be able to tell whether an RS is the audience for a given access token and what data it may receive; otherwise the RS gets nothing for that token. The RFC suggests, for example, keeping a mapping between scope values and resource servers.

One way to do this is to treat every RS as an OAuth client using dynamic client registration (RFC 7591), with at least a client_id and a token_endpoint_auth_method. The AS MUST restrict what such credentials can call, and MAY limit a client to the introspection endpoint only. The AS MAY also encrypt responses, in which case it is provisioned with encryption keys and algorithms for the RS.
sections.eli5: The office handing out answers must know exactly who is asking and which answers that person is allowed to see.

sections.title: Asking For and Getting a JWT
sections.content:
An RS asks for a JWT by sending an introspection request with the Accept header set to application/token-introspection+jwt. The AS MUST authenticate the caller, either with client authentication methods or with a separate access token issued to the RS that identifies it as the subject. An AS that follows this specification MUST refuse to serve introspection requests that do not authenticate the caller and return HTTP status 400, which prevents downgrading to RFC 7662 behavior.

The response sets Content-Type to application/token-introspection+jwt and the JWT typ header to token-introspection+jwt. The JWT MUST contain these top-level claims:

  • iss: the issuer URL of the AS.
  • aud: identifies the RS receiving the response.
  • iat: when the AS created the response.
  • token_introspection: a JSON object holding the members of the RFC 7662 response.

Keeping those members in their own object avoids conflict with same-named top-level JWT claims. If the token is invalid, expired, revoked or not meant for the calling RS, active MUST be false and no other members are included. The AS SHOULD narrow scope to the scopes relevant to that RS. The JWT SHOULD NOT include sub and exp at the top level, as a measure against misuse as an access token.

The JWT in an introspection response is not an alternative representation of the access token and is not meant to be used as one.
sections.eli5: The app asks for the stamped note. The server first checks who is asking, then hands back a stamped note with the answer inside. A wrong or unknown pass just gets "not active".

sections.title: Signing and Encryption Settings
sections.content:
The AS chooses how to secure each response, possibly from metadata the RS registered through dynamic client registration. The RFC defines three client metadata parameters, patterned on OpenID Connect Dynamic Client Registration:

  • introspection_signed_response_alg: the JWS algorithm for signing. The default is RS256.
  • introspection_encrypted_response_alg: the JWE algorithm for content key encryption. By default no encryption is done.
  • introspection_encrypted_response_enc: the JWE algorithm for content encryption. The default is A128CBC-HS256, and it MUST NOT be set without the alg parameter.

If both signing and encryption are requested, the response is signed then encrypted, and the result MUST be a Nested JWT. The AS SHOULD publish what it supports using three authorization server metadata parameters (RFC 8414): introspection_signing_alg_values_supported, introspection_encryption_alg_values_supported and introspection_encryption_enc_values_supported. An RS can register its public encryption keys with jwks_uri or jwks.
sections.eli5: Each app can say how it wants its envelope: just stamped, or stamped and locked in a box. If it says nothing, it gets a stamped one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Two risks are called out. The first is cross-JWT confusion: the iss and possibly aud of an introspection JWT can resemble those of a JWT-encoded access token, so an attacker might pass an introspection response off as an access token. The typ header and the encapsulation of members such as sub and scope inside token_introspection are meant to prevent this. Resource servers MUST check the typ header of received JWT access tokens and ensure all minimally required claims are present, and MUST apply the replay countermeasures in RFC 9700. RFC 8725 discusses JWT confusion further.

The second is token data leakage. The AS MUST use TLS 1.2 or higher, per BCP 195 (RFC 9325), and MUST require all introspection requests to be authenticated, because RFC 7662 allows requests authorized with an access token that does not identify the caller.
sections.eli5: A bad guy might try to use the answer note as if it were the pass itself. A label on the note and a different layout stop that, and every asker must prove who they are.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
An introspection response can carry personal identifiable information from the AS to the RS. Before releasing anything, the AS MUST conform to legal and jurisdictional constraints, which vary and are outside the scope of the document. A common legal basis is explicit user consent gathered during the authorization flow; it can also be established out of band, for example by contract. When the AS and RS belong to the same legal entity, explicit consent may not be needed, but the provider's terms of service and policy MUST still be enforced.

The AS MUST retain the scope of the legal basis with the access token, authenticate the RS, and decide what data the RS may receive from its identity and token data such as the scope value. Introspection also tells the AS when the user is using the client. If that is unacceptable, implementers MUST relay token data by other means, such as putting the needed data in the access token itself.
sections.eli5: If the note has personal details, the office may only share them when it has a good reason, like your permission.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the three client metadata names in the OAuth Dynamic Client Registration Metadata registry and the three server metadata names in the OAuth Authorization Server Metadata registry. It also registered the application/token-introspection+jwt media type, whose intended usage is COMMON, and the token_introspection claim ("Token introspection response") in the JSON Web Token claims registry.
sections.eli5: The new names and the new label were written into the official lists so everyone uses them the same way.
